justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'd assume was the prevailing level at the time of the forecast, somewhere in the low-to-mid 3100s for the S&P 500 or a comparable equity index. For the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the last observed price, expecting mean-reversion tendencies and limited new information to keep the index near its recent close. At one week, I allowed for a slight positive drift reflecting the long-run equity risk premium, while acknowledging that a week is long enough for meaningful macro data releases or Federal Reserve commentary to shift sentiment. At one month, the drift assumption compounds further, but the point estimate remains conservative rather than aggressive, reflecting a broadly neutral near-term macro backdrop without a strong directional catalyst in either direction.

The confidence interval widths are calibrated to typical realized volatility at each time horizon. Daily volatility for large-cap equity indices tends to run around 0.8–1.2% under normal conditions, which translates to the roughly 70-point band I used for the one-day interval. Weekly volatility scales up by roughly the square root of five, and monthly by the square root of roughly 21 trading days, which explains why the one-month interval spans over 500 points. I also gave the intervals a slight asymmetric consideration — equity distributions tend to have fat left tails, meaning large drawdowns are historically more abrupt than equivalent-sized rallies, though I did not heavily skew the intervals in this instance.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes well outside these stated ranges. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in credit markets, a surprise hawkish pivot from the Federal Reserve, a significant geopolitical escalation, or a disappointing earnings season could produce a sharp drawdown that breaks through the lower bound of even the one-month interval. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected easing of inflation, a dovish policy surprise, or a resolution of a major geopolitical overhang could fuel a momentum-driven rally beyond the upper bound. Liquidity events, flash crashes, or systemic financial stress — while low-probability — are the tail risks most likely to invalidate the intervals entirely, particularly at the shorter horizons where such shocks would be most acute relative to the narrow bands assumed.
